To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
A divergent external loop of FT and Tfl1 confers antagonistic activities to these regulators of plant development.
the divergent external loop of FT and TLF1 confers opposite activities on the floral regulators FT and TLFI.
the opposite activities of floral regulators FT and TERMINAL flower1 are determined by a rapidly evolving external loop and a C‐terminal segment.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the mechanisms of action of two key floral regulators in plants.
how the same gene can have opposite activities, and how this difference in function is achieved.
how a single protein can be converted from a floral repressor to a floral inducer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the external loop of the TFL1‐type protein is responsible for the antagonistic activity of FT and TDL1.
the external loop of FT and Tfl1 is the most important determinant of their opposite activities.

FT and TFL are both transcription factors that are recruited to the promoter of floral genes through an interaction with FD, but that FT and TLF1 have opposite effects on flowering, which can be mapped to a 14 amino acid segment that is highly variable among plant species.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a small region of the protein that is variable in TFL1 is not variable in FT.
a small, rapidly evolving segment of TFL1 is responsible for its antagonistic activity to FT.
the external loop of TFL1 and the C‐terminal peptide of FT are important for the antagonistic activities of FT and/or TFL.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the divergent loop is a major determinant of the opposite FT and/or TFL activities.
the opposite functions of FT and TLF1 are conferred in part by a single divergent loop.
a single amino acid change can alter the activity of a transcription factor, and that this can be accomplished through a change in the conformation and/or accessibility of a surface of the protein.
